seo_title: Grade 8 Math: Tessellations and Transformations Worksheets (Free, Ontario Curriculum, Answer Key)
standard_text: Describe and perform translations, reflections, rotations, and dilations on a Cartesian plane, and predict the results of these transformations
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 math worksheets on tessellations and transformations for the Ontario curriculum: which shapes tessellate (angles at a point add to 360°), transformations in tile patterns, translations, reflections, rotations and dilations on the Cartesian plane, and predicting the results. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: A shape tessellates when the angles meeting at each point add up to 360°. On the plane, every vertex moves by the same rule.
key_sub: Equilateral triangles (6 × 60°), squares (4 × 90°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°) tessellate; regular pentagons (108°) do not. Rotation about the origin: 90° clockwise (x, y) → (y, −x), 90° counterclockwise (−y, x), 180° (−x, −y). Dilation by k: (kx, ky).
body_html:
Tessellations

A shape tessellates when copies of it cover a surface with no gaps and no overlaps. Where corners meet, the angles must add up to 360°. Each angle of a regular polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n.

Regular polygonEach angleAround a pointTessellates on its own?
equilateral triangle60°6 × 60° = 360°yes
square90°4 × 90° = 360°yes
regular hexagon120°3 × 120° = 360°yes
regular pentagon108°3 × 108° = 324° (gap)no
regular octagon135°2 × 135° = 270° (gap)no

Any triangle and any quadrilateral tessellates. Two shapes can also tessellate together: 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.

Every tessellation is built with transformations. Tiles that face the same way are translations of each other. Mirror-image tiles come from reflections, and turned tiles from rotations.

Example

Two regular hexagons meet at a point. How many equilateral triangles fill the gap?

2 × 120° = 240°. 360° − 240° = 120°. 120° ÷ 60° = 2.

Answer: 2 triangles

Transformations on the Cartesian plane

Move every vertex with the same rule, then join the new vertices. Translations, reflections and rotations keep the size, so the image is congruent. A dilation changes the size, so the image is similar.

TransformationRule for (x, y)
Translation a right and b up(x + a, y + b)
Reflection in the x-axis(x, −y)
Reflection in the y-axis(−x, y)
Rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin(y, −x)
Rotation of 90° counterclockwise about the origin(−y, x)
Rotation of 180° about the origin(−x, −y)
Dilation by scale factor k, centre at the origin(kx, ky)
Example

Reflect (5, 3) in the line x = 2.

(5, 3) is 3 units right of the line, so the image is 3 units left of it: x = 2 − 3 = −1. y stays 3.

Answer: (−1, 3)

For a 90° turn, swap the two numbers, then change one sign. Clockwise (the way clock hands move): change the sign of the second number. Counterclockwise: change the sign of the first number.

Example

Rotate (2, 5) 90° counterclockwise about the origin.

Swap: (5, 2). Change the sign of the first number: (−5, 2). Check: Quadrant I turns counterclockwise into Quadrant II.

Answer: (−5, 2)

Dilations

A dilation with the centre at the origin multiplies both coordinates by the scale factor. A scale factor greater than 1 enlarges the shape; a scale factor between 0 and 1 shrinks it. The angles stay the same.

Example

Dilate (−9, 6) by a scale factor of 13.

Divide both coordinates by 3: −9 ÷ 3 = −3 and 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

Answer: (−3, 2)

Combining and predicting

Do the steps in order and follow one vertex. The order can change the answer. Predict first, then check: a reflection in the x-axis moves a point up or down to the other side, a 180° rotation sends it to the opposite quadrant, and a dilation keeps it in the same quadrant.

Example

Reflect (2, 3) in the x-axis, then translate it 4 units up.

(2, 3) → (2, −3) → (2, 1). Doing the steps the other way gives (2, −7).

Answer: (2, 1)

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking all regular polygons tessellateOnly triangles, squares and hexagons: their angles divide exactly into 360°
Rotating the wrong wayClockwise goes the way clock hands move: from the top to the right
Only swapping the numbers in a 90° turn: (3, 1) → (1, 3)Swap and change one sign: (1, −3) clockwise, (−1, 3) counterclockwise
Reflecting in the wrong axisIn the x-axis, y changes sign. In the y-axis, x changes sign
Adding the scale factor: (4, −5) by 3 → (7, −2)Multiply both coordinates: (12, −15)
Doing the steps of a combination in a different orderFollow the order given, one step at a time

faq.q: What do Grade 8 students learn about transformations in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: In Grade 8 Spatial Sense, students perform translations, reflections, rotations and dilations on the Cartesian plane and predict the results. They also study which shapes tessellate and the transformations used in tessellations.

faq.q: Why does a regular pentagon not tessellate?
faq.a: Each angle is 108°. Three pentagons make 324°, leaving a 36° gap, and four make 432°, which overlaps, so they cannot fill the 360° around a point.

faq.q: How do you rotate a point 90° about the origin?
faq.a: Swap the two numbers, then change one sign. For 90° clockwise, (x, y) becomes (y, −x); for 90° counterclockwise, it becomes (−y, x).

faq.q: Is there a provincial math test in Grade 8 in Ontario?
faq.a: No. EQAO math assessments are written in Grades 3 and 6, and the next one is in Grade 9. These worksheets help Grade 8 students practise for class tests and get ready for high school.

sets.title: Which shapes tessellate? Angles at a point

items.q: In a tessellation, what do the angles that meet at a point add up to?
items.e: The tiles go all the way around the point with no gaps and no overlaps: a full turn, 360°. (180° is the sum of the angles on a straight line or in a triangle.)

items.q: Each angle of a square is 90°. How many squares fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 90° = 4, so 4 squares fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°. How many equilateral triangles fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 60° = 6, so 6 equilateral triangles fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°. How many regular hexagons fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 120° = 3, so 3 regular hexagons fit exactly around each point.

items.q: What is the size of each angle of a regular pentagon?
items.e: The angles of a pentagon add up to (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°. A regular pentagon has 5 equal angles: 540° ÷ 5 = 108°. (72° is the turn at each corner as you walk around it, and 540° is the total.)

items.q: What is the size of each angle of a regular octagon?
items.e: The angles of an octagon add up to (8 − 2) × 180° = 1080°. 1080° ÷ 8 = 135°. (45° is the turn at each corner, 1080° is the total, and 120° is the angle of a regular hexagon.)

items.q: Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. Do regular pentagons tessellate on their own?
items.e: 3 × 108° = 324°, which is less than 360°, so there is a gap. 4 × 108° = 432°, which is more than 360°, so a fourth pentagon would overlap. Regular pentagons do not tessellate.

items.q: Three regular pentagons meet at the red dot. Each angle is 108°. What is the size of the gap?
items.e: 3 × 108° = 324°. A full turn is 360°, so the gap is 360° − 324° = 36°. No regular polygon has a 36° angle.

items.q: Each angle of a regular octagon is 135°. Why do regular octagons not tessellate on their own?
items.e: Around a point the angles must add up to exactly 360°. 2 × 135° = 270° leaves a gap and 3 × 135° = 405° is too much. 135° does not divide exactly into 360°. (Regular hexagons have obtuse angles too, and they do tessellate.)

items.q: Which shape tessellates on its own?
items.e: The regular hexagon (A): each angle is 120° and 3 × 120° = 360°. A regular pentagon (108°) and a regular octagon (135°) leave gaps, and circles cannot fit together without gaps.

items.q: Which shape does NOT tessellate on its own?
items.e: The regular pentagon (D): 360° ÷ 108° is not a whole number. Squares (4 × 90°), equilateral triangles (6 × 60°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°) all fit exactly around a point.

items.q: Which regular polygons tessellate on their own?
c: Every regular polygon with an even number of sides
Only equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons
items.e: A regular polygon tessellates only if its angle divides exactly into 360°: 60° (6 fit), 90° (4 fit) and 120° (3 fit). Regular pentagons (108°) and octagons (135°) do not, even though an octagon has an even number of sides.

items.q: Leah says, “All regular polygons tessellate.” Which shape shows that she is wrong?
items.e: Regular pentagons leave a 36° gap around a point (3 × 108° = 324°). Squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons do tessellate, so they cannot show that Leah is wrong.

items.q: Copies of any triangle tessellate. A triangle has angles of 40°, 60° and 80°. In its tessellation, each angle appears twice at every meeting point. How many triangles meet at each point?
items.e: Each angle appears twice: 2 × (40° + 60° + 80°) = 2 × 180° = 360°. That is 6 angles, so 6 triangles meet at each point. (3 triangles give only 180°.)

items.q: Does every quadrilateral (even an irregular one) tessellate?
c: No: its sides must be equal
Only if it has a right angle
No: only squares and rectangles do
Yes: its four angles add up to 360°
items.e: The angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360°. Put one copy of each angle around a point and they fill it exactly, so any quadrilateral tessellates.

items.q: Two regular octagons meet at the red dot. Each angle is 135°. What is the size of the gap?
items.e: 2 × 135° = 270°, and 360° − 270° = 90°. A square fits the gap exactly, so octagons and squares tessellate together.

items.q: Two regular hexagons meet at the red dot. How many equilateral triangles fill the gap?
items.e: 2 × 120° = 240°, so the gap is 360° − 240° = 120°. Each equilateral triangle has 60° angles: 120° ÷ 60° = 2 triangles.

items.q: Two squares meet at a point. How many equilateral triangles fill the rest of the space around the point?
items.e: 2 × 90° = 180°, so 360° − 180° = 180° is left. 180° ÷ 60° = 3 equilateral triangles.

items.q: At each corner of a tiling, a regular hexagon, two squares and one more regular polygon meet. What is the angle of the missing polygon?
items.e: 120° + 90° + 90° = 300°. 360° − 300° = 60°, so the missing tile is an equilateral triangle. (150° forgets the second square.)

items.q: Each angle of a regular dodecagon (12 sides) is 150°. Does it tessellate on its own?
c: Yes: it has an even number of sides
items.e: 2 × 150° = 300° leaves a 60° gap and 3 × 150° = 450° overlaps. 360° ÷ 150° is not a whole number, so it does not tessellate on its own. (An equilateral triangle could fill the 60° gap.)

items.q: In this brick wall, how is each row placed compared with the row below it?
items.e: Each row is the row below slid half a brick sideways and up one row. Nothing is flipped or turned, so it is a translation.

items.q: How many hexagons meet at the red dot?
items.e: 3 hexagons meet at each corner. Each angle is 120°, and 3 × 120° = 360°.

items.q: How many triangles meet at the red dot?
items.e: 6 triangles meet at each point. Each angle is 60°, and 6 × 60° = 360°.

items.q: Which two shapes make this floor tile pattern?
items.e: The large tiles have 8 equal sides (regular octagons) and the small tiles are squares turned on an angle. At each corner, 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.

items.q: How many tiles meet at the red dot?
items.e: 2 octagons and 1 square meet at each corner: 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Every flag points the same way and is the same way up. Each one is the one before slid 1 tile to the right.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: The flags point right, left, right, left but stay the same way up: each is a mirror image of the one before, with the mirror line on the edge between the tiles. A rotation of 180° would also turn it upside down.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Each flag is upside down and points the other way. It is the one before rotated 180° about the middle of the edge between the tiles. A reflection flips it only one way.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Each flag is upside down but still points right. It is reflected in the line across the middle of the strip and then slid 1 tile along, like a trail of footprints.

items.q: Each tile is the tile before rotated 90° clockwise. Which tile comes next?
items.e: The flag on the pole points right, then down, then left. One more turn of 90° clockwise makes it point up: A. The others: B: it is a mirror image of the right answer, flipped, not turned; C: it is turned counterclockwise, back to the second tile; D: it is turned 90° too far, back to the start.

items.q: Which pattern is a tessellation?
items.e: A tessellation has no gaps and no overlaps. Only the squares (D) fit together with no gaps. The others: A: the pentagons leave a gap; B: the circles leave curved gaps; C: the octagons leave square gaps.

items.q: This quilt block has 4 small squares. Going around clockwise, how is each small square made from the one before it?
c: a rotation of 90° clockwise about the centre of the block
a reflection in the line between them
a rotation of 180° about the centre of the block
items.e: Look at the long side of each red triangle: it lies along the top of the block, then the right side, then the bottom, then the left. Each square is the one before rotated 90° clockwise about the centre. A reflection would make a mirror image.

items.q: An artist cuts a bump out of the left side of a square tile and attaches the same bump to the right side, without turning it. Will copies of the new tile still tessellate?
c: No: curved edges always leave gaps
Only if the bump is cut off again
Yes: each bump fits into the gap in the next tile
items.e: The bump was translated from one side to the opposite side, so the gap matches the bump exactly. The artist M. C. Escher used this idea to make tessellations of birds, fish and lizards.

items.q: A triangle is rotated 180° about the midpoint of one of its sides. What shape do the triangle and its image make together?
items.e: The 180° rotation puts a copy of the triangle against the same side, upside down. Together they make a parallelogram. Rows of parallelograms tessellate, which is why every triangle tessellates.

items.q: In a tessellation of an irregular quadrilateral, which transformation maps a tile onto the tile that shares one of its sides?
c: a rotation of 180° about the midpoint of that side
a dilation by a scale factor of 2
a rotation of 90° about a corner
items.e: Turning the tile 180° about the midpoint of a side puts the same side back in place, with the matching angles beside each other. A reflection of an irregular shape would not fit the pattern, and a dilation changes the size.

items.q: A trail of footprints in fresh snow goes left foot, right foot, left foot, right foot. How is each footprint made from the one before?
items.e: A right foot is a mirror image of a left foot, so there is a reflection. The footprint is also further along the path, so there is a translation too.

items.q: Hana rotates a square tile 90° about one corner, again and again. How many tiles fit around that corner?
items.e: Each turn is 90°. 360° ÷ 90° = 4, so 4 tiles fill the space around the corner.

items.q: Which tile could NOT be used on its own to cover a floor with no gaps?
items.e: Regular octagons (135°) leave square gaps, which is why octagon floors have small square tiles between them. Rectangles, regular hexagons and equilateral triangles cover a floor on their own.

items.q: A design has 1 regular hexagon and some equilateral triangles at every corner. How many triangles are at each corner?
items.e: The hexagon’s angle is 120°, so 360° − 120° = 240° is left. 240° ÷ 60° = 4 triangles.

items.q: In a honeycomb pattern, which transformation moves a hexagon onto the next hexagon in the same row?
items.e: All the hexagons face the same way, so each one is the one before slid along: a translation. A 90° turn would not put a hexagon onto its neighbour, and a dilation changes the size.

items.q: Translate (−3, 4) 6 units right and 7 units down. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Translate 6 units right and 7 units down: x: −3 + 6 = 3, y: 4 − 7 = −3. (−3, 4) → (3, −3).

items.q: A point moves from (−5, 2) to (3, −4). Describe the translation.
items.e: Find the change: new minus old. x: 3 − (−5) = 8, so 8 units right; y: −4 − 2 = −6, so 6 units down. The translation is 8 units right and 6 units down. The move crosses the y-axis, so the sizes add: 5 + 3 = 8.

items.q: Which rule shows a translation 4 units left and 3 units up?
items.e: Left subtracts from x: x − 4. Up adds to y: y + 3. So (x, y) → (x − 4, y + 3).

items.q: Reflect (−6, 5) in the x-axis. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Reflect in the x-axis: x stays, y changes sign. (−6, 5) → (−6, −5).

items.q: Reflect (4, −2) in the y-axis. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Reflect in the y-axis: y stays, x changes sign. (4, −2) → (−4, −2).

items.q: Reflect (5, 3) in the line x = 2. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: (5, 3) is 3 units right of the line x = 2, so the image is 3 units left of it: x = 2 − 3 = −1. y stays 3. (5, 3) → (−1, 3). ((−5, 3) is the reflection in the y-axis, not in x = 2.)

items.q: Reflect (−4, 6) in the line y = 1. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: (−4, 6) is 5 units above the line y = 1, so the image is 5 units below it: y = 1 − 5 = −4. x stays −4. (−4, 6) → (−4, −4). ((−4, −6) is the reflection in the x-axis, not in y = 1.)

items.q: Which point is the reflection of point P in the y-axis?
items.e: P is at (−5, −3). Reflect in the y-axis: y stays, x changes sign. (−5, −3) → (5, −3). That is point C. Point A is the reflection in the x-axis instead, and point B changes both signs.

items.q: Triangle B is the reflection of triangle A. Which axis is the mirror line?
items.e: Compare a vertex and its image: (−2, 1) → (−2, −1). x stays the same and y changes sign, so the shape flipped up or down. The mirror line is the x-axis.

items.q: Rotate (5, 2) 90° clockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Rotate 90° clockwise: (x, y) → (y, −x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the second one. (5, 2) → (2, −5).

items.q: Rotate (−3, −4) 90° counterclockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Rotate 90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the first one. (−3, −4) → (4, −3).

items.q: Rotate (−6, 1) 180° about the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Rotate 180°: both signs change. (−6, 1) → (6, −1).

items.q: Rotate (2, 6) 270° clockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: 270° clockwise is 90° short of a full turn, so it ends in the same place as 90° counterclockwise. Rotate 90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the first one. (2, 6) → (−6, 2).

items.q: Point P is rotated 90° clockwise about the origin. Which point is the image?
items.e: P is at (4, 3). Rotate 90° clockwise: (x, y) → (y, −x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the second one. (4, 3) → (3, −4). That is point D. Point A is a turn the wrong way, and point B only swaps the numbers.

items.q: Triangle A is rotated about the origin to give triangle B. Describe the rotation.
items.e: Follow one vertex. Rotate 90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the first one. (5, 2) → (−2, 5). The shape turned a quarter turn counterclockwise about the origin.

items.q: A triangle has vertices (1, 2), (4, 2), (4, 5). It is rotated 180° about the origin. What are the vertices of the image?
items.e: A 180° rotation changes both signs of every vertex: (1, 2), (4, 2), (4, 5) → (−1, −2), (−4, −2), (−4, −5).

items.q: Aiden rotates (3, 1) 90° counterclockwise about the origin and gets (1, −3). What mistake did he make?
items.e: Aiden used the clockwise rule (y, −x). Counterclockwise is the opposite way to clock hands. Rotate 90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the first one. (3, 1) → (−1, 3).

items.q: Point (−5, −2) is rotated 90° clockwise about the origin. Which quadrant is the image in?
items.e: (−5, −2) is in Quadrant III. A quarter turn clockwise moves it to the next quadrant clockwise: Quadrant II. Check: the image is (−2, 5).

items.q: A transformation follows the rule (x, y) → (−x, y). What is it?
items.e: Only x changes sign, so each point flips left or right across the y-axis. Example: (3, 2) → (−3, 2).

items.q: A transformation follows the rule (x, y) → (−x, −y). What is it?
items.e: Both signs change and the numbers stay in the same order. That is a half turn about the origin. Example: (3, 2) → (−3, −2). (A reflection changes only one sign.)

items.q: Dilate (3, −2) by a scale factor of 2 with the centre at the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Dilate by 2: multiply both coordinates by 2. 3 × 2 = 6 and −2 × 2 = −4. (3, −2) → (6, −4).

items.q: Dilate (−2, 4) by a scale factor of 3 with the centre at the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Dilate by 3: multiply both coordinates by 3. −2 × 3 = −6 and 4 × 3 = 12. (−2, 4) → (−6, 12).

items.q: Dilate (8, −6) by a scale factor of 12 with the centre at the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Dilate by 12: multiply both coordinates by 12, which is the same as dividing by 2. 8 ÷ 2 = 4 and −6 ÷ 2 = −3. (8, −6) → (4, −3).

items.q: Dilate (−9, 6) by a scale factor of 13 with the centre at the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Dilate by 13: multiply both coordinates by 13, which is the same as dividing by 3. −9 ÷ 3 = −3 and 6 ÷ 3 = 2. (−9, 6) → (−3, 2).

items.q: Dilate (−5, 1) by a scale factor of 4 with the centre at the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Dilate by 4: multiply both coordinates by 4. −5 × 4 = −20 and 1 × 4 = 4. (−5, 1) → (−20, 4).

items.q: Dilate (4, −2) by a scale factor of 32 with the centre at the origin. What are the coordinates of the image?
items.e: Dilate by 32: divide each coordinate by 2, then multiply by 3. 4 ÷ 2 × 3 = 6 and −2 ÷ 2 × 3 = −3. (4, −2) → (6, −3). ((12, −6) multiplies by 3 but forgets to divide by 2, and (2, −1) divides by 2 only.)

items.q: Point P is dilated by a scale factor of 2 with the centre at the origin. Which point is the image?
items.e: P is at (2, −3). Dilate by 2: multiply both coordinates by 2. 2 × 2 = 4 and −3 × 2 = −6. (2, −3) → (4, −6). That is point C. Point A comes from adding 2 instead of multiplying, and points B and D multiply only one coordinate.

items.q: Point P is dilated by a scale factor of 3 with the centre at the origin. Which point is the image?
items.e: P is at (−2, 1). Dilate by 3: multiply both coordinates by 3. −2 × 3 = −6 and 1 × 3 = 3. (−2, 1) → (−6, 3). That is point B. Point A comes from adding 3 instead of multiplying, and points C and D multiply only one coordinate.

items.q: Triangle B is a dilation of triangle A with the centre at the origin. What is the scale factor?
items.e: Compare a vertex and its image: (3, 1) → (6, 2). Each coordinate is multiplied by 2. Check a side: the bottom side of A is 2 units long and the bottom side of B is 4 units long. B is bigger, so the scale factor is more than 1.

items.q: Triangle B is a dilation of triangle A with the centre at the origin. What is the scale factor?
items.e: Compare a vertex and its image: (6, 4) → (3, 2). Each coordinate is multiplied by 12. Check a side: the bottom side of A is 4 units long and the bottom side of B is 2 units long. B is smaller, so the scale factor is less than 1.

items.q: A rectangle has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2), (1, 2). It is dilated by a scale factor of 3 with the centre at the origin. What are the vertices of the image?
items.e: Multiply both coordinates of every vertex by 3: (1, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2), (1, 2) → (3, 3), (9, 3), (9, 6), (3, 6). (Adding 3 slides the rectangle but keeps its size.)

items.q: Point (9, −6) is dilated with the centre at the origin, and its image is (3, −2). What is the scale factor?
items.e: Image ÷ original: 3 ÷ 9 = 13 and −2 ÷ (−6) = 13. Both coordinates are divided by 3, so the scale factor is 13. (3 takes the image back to the original, and 6 and 4 are the changes in x and y, not a scale factor.)

items.q: A rectangle is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. It is dilated by a scale factor of 1.5. What are the length and width of the image?
items.e: Multiply every length by 1.5: 6 × 1.5 = 9 cm and 4 × 1.5 = 6 cm. Adding 1.5 to each side (7.5 cm and 5.5 cm) does not keep the same shape.

items.q: A triangle has an angle of 72°. It is dilated by a scale factor of 12. What is the matching angle in the image?
items.e: A dilation changes the side lengths, not the angles. Matching angles in similar shapes are equal, so the angle is still 72°.

items.q: A triangle has a perimeter of 24 cm. It is dilated by a scale factor of 13. What is the perimeter of the image?
items.e: Every side is multiplied by 13, so the perimeter is too: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 cm. (72 cm multiplies by 3, and 21 cm subtracts 3.)

items.q: A square with sides of 3 cm is dilated by a scale factor of 2. What is the area of the image?
items.e: The image has sides of 3 × 2 = 6 cm, so its area is 6 × 6 = 36 cm². That is 4 times the old area of 9 cm², not 2 times (18 cm²). (24 cm is the perimeter of the image, not its area.)

items.q: A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. Which triangle is similar to it?
items.e: Similar shapes have every side multiplied by the same scale factor. 6 × 1.5 = 9, 8 × 1.5 = 12 and 10 × 1.5 = 15. Adding the same amount (8, 10, 12) or scaling only some sides (9, 12, 10) does not give a similar triangle.

items.q: Zoe dilates (−4, 6) by a scale factor of 12 with the centre at the origin and gets (−8, 12). What mistake did she make?
c: She multiplied by 2 instead of by 12
She added 12 to each coordinate
items.e: Zoe doubled both coordinates. A scale factor of 12 halves them. Dilate by 12: multiply both coordinates by 12, which is the same as dividing by 2. −4 ÷ 2 = −2 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3. (−4, 6) → (−2, 3).

items.q: Which scale factor makes the image smaller than the original shape?
items.e: A scale factor between 0 and 1 shrinks the shape: 13 makes every side a third as long. A scale factor of 1 keeps the same size, and 32 or 3 enlarges it.

items.q: Point A is dilated by a scale factor of 3 with the centre at the origin. The image is (−6, 9). Where is point A?
items.e: Undo the dilation: divide both coordinates by 3. −6 ÷ 3 = −2 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3, so A is (−2, 3). Check: Dilate by 3: multiply both coordinates by 3. −2 × 3 = −6 and 3 × 3 = 9. (−2, 3) → (−6, 9).

items.q: Which single transformation maps triangle A onto triangle B?
items.e: Triangle B is the same size and faces the same way as triangle A: it only slid. That is a translation (6 units right and 5 units down).

items.q: Which single transformation maps triangle A onto triangle B?
items.e: Follow one vertex. Reflect in the y-axis: y stays, x changes sign. (−2, 2) → (2, 2). Check the other vertices: they all land on triangle B, so it is a reflection in the y-axis.

items.q: Which single transformation maps triangle A onto triangle B?
items.e: Follow one vertex. Rotate 180°: both signs change. (5, 2) → (−5, −2). Check the other vertices: they all land on triangle B, so it is a rotation of 180°.

items.q: Which single transformation maps triangle A onto triangle B?
items.e: Triangle B has the same shape as triangle A but is bigger, so it is a dilation. Dilate by 3: multiply both coordinates by 3. 2 × 3 = 6 and 1 × 3 = 3. (2, 1) → (6, 3). Translations, reflections and rotations never change the size.

items.q: Triangle PQR has vertices (2, 1), (5, 1), (5, 3). Its image has vertices (−1, 2), (−1, 5), (−3, 5), in the same order. Which single transformation was used?
items.e: Compare each vertex with its image. Rotate 90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the first one. (2, 1) → (−1, 2). The rule works for every vertex, so it is a rotation of 90° counterclockwise.

items.q: Point (4, 1) is rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin, then translated 3 units right. Where does it end up?
items.e: Do the steps in order. Rotate 90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the first one. (4, 1) → (−1, 4). Translate 3 units right: x: −1 + 3 = 2, y stays 4. (−1, 4) → (2, 4). (Translating first gives (−1, 7): the order matters.)

items.q: A point moves from (4, −2) to (−4, 2). Noah says it was a rotation of 180° about the origin. Amira says it was a reflection in the x-axis, then a reflection in the y-axis. Who is right?
items.e: 180° rotation: both signs change, (4, −2) → (−4, 2). Two reflections: (4, −2) → (4, 2) → (−4, 2). Both give the same image.

items.q: Point (2, 3) is reflected in the x-axis and translated 4 units up. Does the order of the two steps matter?
c: Yes, but only the x-coordinate changes
items.e: Reflect first: (2, 3) → (2, −3) → (2, 1). Translate first: (2, 3) → (2, 7) → (2, −7). The answers are different, so do the steps in the order given.

items.q: A point in Quadrant II is reflected in the x-axis, then rotated 180° about the origin. Predict the quadrant of the final image.
items.e: Reflecting in the x-axis takes Quadrant II (left, up) to Quadrant III (left, down). A 180° rotation takes it to the opposite quadrant: Quadrant I. Example: (−3, 2) → (−3, −2) → (3, 2).

items.q: A triangle is in Quadrant IV. It is dilated by a scale factor of 2 with the centre at the origin. Predict the quadrant of the image.
items.e: Multiplying by a positive scale factor keeps both signs, so the image stays in Quadrant IV, twice as far from the origin. Example: (2, −1) → (4, −2).

items.q: A drone video of a park in Winnipeg uses a grid with the origin at the fountain, east to the right and north up. The drone is at (−4, −3). It flies 7 units east and 5 units north. Where is it now?
items.e: Translate 7 units right and 5 units up: x: −4 + 7 = 3, y: −3 + 5 = 2. (−4, −3) → (3, 2).

items.q: A ringette coach draws a drill on a grid with the origin at the centre of the rink. A player starts at (5, −2). The coach copies the drill to the other side of the rink by reflecting it in the x-axis. Where is the player’s image?
items.e: Reflect in the x-axis: x stays, y changes sign. (5, −2) → (5, 2).

items.q: A robotics club programs a robot arm that turns about the origin. The gripper is at (3, 4). The arm turns 90° clockwise. Where is the gripper now?
items.e: Rotate 90° clockwise: (x, y) → (y, −x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the second one. (3, 4) → (4, −3).

items.q: A school yearbook photo is 5 cm wide and 7 cm tall. It is enlarged by a scale factor of 3 for a poster in the gym. What size is the enlarged photo?
items.e: Multiply both lengths by 3: 5 × 3 = 15 cm and 7 × 3 = 21 cm. Adding 3 (8 cm by 10 cm) would stretch the photo out of shape.

items.q: Lucas draws a maple leaf design for a sticker. One tip is at (−8, 6). He dilates the design by a scale factor of 12 with the centre at the origin. Where is that tip now?
items.e: Dilate by 12: multiply both coordinates by 12, which is the same as dividing by 2. −8 ÷ 2 = −4 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3. (−8, 6) → (−4, 3).

items.q: The CN Tower is 553 m tall. A model of it is a dilation with a scale factor of 11000. How tall is the model?
items.e: 553 m ÷ 1000 = 0.553 m. Change to centimetres: 0.553 × 100 = 55.3 cm. (55.3 m divides by 10 only; 553 cm and 5.53 cm move the decimal point the wrong number of places.)

items.q: Emma plans a snow sculpture on a grid. A corner on the small plan is at (3, −2), and the same corner on the full-size plan is at (12, −8). The full-size plan is a dilation of the small one with the centre at the origin. What is the scale factor?
items.e: Image ÷ original: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and −8 ÷ (−2) = 4. The scale factor is 4. (9 and 6 are the changes in x and y; 14 would shrink the plan.)

items.q: In a video game, Maya’s character is rotated 90° clockwise about the origin and ends at (−3, 5). Where did it start?
items.e: Undo the turn by turning the other way. Rotate 90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the first one. (−3, 5) → (−5, −3). Check: Rotate 90° clockwise: (x, y) → (y, −x). Swap the numbers, then change the sign of the second one. (−5, −3) → (−3, 5).

items.q: Olivia is designing floor tiles for a community centre in Ottawa. Each corner must have 2 regular octagons and one other regular tile. Which tile fills the space?
items.e: 2 × 135° = 270°, so 360° − 270° = 90° is left. A square has 90° angles, so it fits exactly.

items.q: In a coding app, Owen moves a sprite from (−1, 3) 5 units left and 2 units up, then 3 units right and 6 units down. Which single translation does the same?
items.e: Add the moves. x: −5 + 3 = −2, so 2 units left. y: 2 + (−6) = −4, so 4 units down. Check: (−1, 3) → (−3, −1).
